title: Aurora Cloud - Redwood Private/VPC Discovery
summary: Discovery call to understand Aurora Cloud's networking constraints for a Redwood Private (VPC) deployment. Key topics: VPC peering vs PrivateLink, cross-account peering limits, region/residency requirements, routing and NAT, KMS/HSM integration, control plane connectivity, and pilot scope. Next steps: share VPC template, architecture diagram, security pack, and schedule a network deep-dive with Aurora's cloud infra team.
next_steps: Send VPC design template and example CloudFormation/Terraform
Share security pack (SOC2 docs, SSO/SAML guide, KMS notes)
Schedule network deep-dive with Aurora infra team next week
Spin up a short POC for 2 models and run latency benchmarks in us-east-1 and eu-west-1
action_items: Maya Chen - share architecture diagram and VPC template - due 2027-09-16
Rafael Ortega - prepare pilot runbook and sample benchmark script - due 2027-09-18
Priya Singh / Aurora - provide list of IP ranges and account IDs for peering - due 2027-09-17
Omar Khalid / Aurora - confirm region constraints and legal residency requirements - due 2027-09-20
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-14
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Rafael Ortega (Redwood SE), Lena Park (CTO, Aurora Cloud), Omar Khalid (Infra Lead), Priya Singh (Security), Ben Carter (SRE)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, and Rafael our solutions engineer is with me. Quick intro, then we wanted to dig into your VPC requirements.
[00:12] Lena Park: Hi, thanks. I'll keep it short. We're Aurora Cloud, we run regionally distributed cloud infra for B2B SaaS. We're evaluating Redwood Private for model serving inside our VPCs. Key constraints are multi-account architecture, EU data residency, and very strict egress controls.
[00:27] Omar Khalid: Yeah we need to make sure whatever we do doesn't open out to the public internet except for specific update windows.
[00:33] Rafael Ortega: Got it. The core decision we usually help teams with is whether to use VPC peering/transit gateway or PrivateLink (AWS PrivateLink / Azure Private Endpoint). Both have tradeoffs — peering is simpler but hits account/peer limits and can be messy for multi-account topologies; PrivateLink gives you an endpoint in your VPC but requires NLBs and cross-account endpoint services.
[00:52] Priya Singh: A couple questions up front — do you support customer-managed KMS keys? We need all at-rest encryption under our key, and HSM-backed if possible. Also need detailed audit logs and SSO integration.
[01:05] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood Private supports customer KMS/HSM integrations — we have references for AWS KMS and HSM setups; we'll send our security pack. For SSO we support SAML/SSO and RBAC mapping. Audit logs can be shipped to your logging endpoints or forwarded to your SIEM.
[01:22] Ben Carter: For the networking bit — do you require an outbound NAT for model downloads or image pulls during bootstrap?
[01:28] Rafael Ortega: There are two parts: control plane and data plane. In our Private offering, control plane can be configured as a private control plane in your VPC or as a managed control plane that still needs an egress path for updates. For a fully air-gapped on-prem, we provide an on-prem package but for VPC deployments typically you allow limited egress to Redwood update endpoints (we can whitelist IPs). For image/model pulls we can either pre-stage models in your S3/registry or pull from our model registry via private connectivity.
[01:52] Speaker 6: (mumbling) pre-stage would be preferred...
[01:57] Omar Khalid: Important for us — we operate multiple AWS accounts per region, and we use a transit gateway. How does Redwood handle multi-account peering? If you do VPC peering we could quickly hit limits.
[02:10] Rafael Ortega: Right — we typically recommend PrivateLink for multi-account setups with many VPCs because it avoids N-to-N peering. If you're using a Transit Gateway, we can integrate via a service VPC behind an NLB and expose endpoints to consumer VPCs using PrivateLink, or we can request peering from each account to the Redwood service VPC. Transit Gateway integration is common; a couple caveats: route table propagation and to make sure your TGW attachments allow the flow.
[02:36] Lena Park: How about cross-region? We need EU data to stay in eu-west-1 and some US things in us-east-1. Can we pin models/traffic regionally?
[02:45] Maya Chen: Absolutely — we support regional deployments. For Private you can choose the region/availability zone you'd like the deployment in. If you need separate control planes in EU and US we can do that — usually customers run separate private deployments per region and Redwood's routing rules keep requests routed to the region-specific model serving.
[03:02] Priya Singh: Any known restrictions with Azure or GCP if we have multi-cloud?
[03:07] Rafael Ortega: We primarily support AWS PrivateLink patterns and transit gateway for AWS at the moment. For Azure and GCP we use their equivalents — Azure Private Endpoint and GCP Private Service Connect. Some features like cross-region private link can be more limited; we'll document for your exact multi-cloud topology in the follow-up.
[03:24] Ben Carter: Let's talk IP whitelisting and DNS. We use internal DNS zones per account and expect resolvable private endpoints. Do you require us to update route tables or DNS forwarders?
[03:34] Rafael Ortega: For PrivateLink you get an endpoint ENI in your subnet and DNS entries get created via the endpoint service — you can control private hosted zone integration. For peering, you'll need route table entries for the peered CIDRs. We can provide Terraform examples that show route table changes and security group rules.
[03:51] Lena Park: Also curious about certificate management for TLS and mTLS between our services and Redwood.
[03:56] Maya Chen: We support mTLS for data plane if you require mutual TLS; otherwise standard TLS with customer key management is available. If you want hardware-backed keys, we integrate with KMS/HSM for signing and encryption.
[04:10] Omar Khalid: What about throughput and latency — if we colocate in eu-west-1 with our services, what's typical token latency  for request/response? We benchmark for 512-token prompts primarily.
[04:21] Rafael Ortega: Typically in-region with dedicated capacity you'll see sub-100ms per-token overhead depending on model size — but depends a lot on batching and KV cache patterns. For the pilot we can run a 512-token synthetic load to measure p99 latency. We'll include a benchmark script.
[04:36] Priya Singh: On compliance — we need SOC2 report and encryption details for legal review. Can you provide those?
[04:41] Maya Chen: Yes we'll attach our SOC2 and ISO documents in the security pack. We'll also outline audit log retention options and how logs are forwarded.
[04:50] Speaker 6: (crosstalk) the team also wanted to know about patching and software updates — do you push runtime updates into our VPC?
[04:57] Rafael Ortega: If you run the Redwood Private managed deployment, updates can be scheduled — we can either do rolling updates using internal images pulled through your approved egress path, or we can hand over update artifacts for you to apply. For strict environments we recommend the latter with a scheduled maintenance window.
[05:15] Lena Park: Important: Our security team won't accept any outbound connection that isn't explicitly whitelisted. We also require all KMS keys to be customer-owned.
[05:23] Maya Chen: That's fine; many customers require the same. We'll send the minimal list of IPs and domains to whitelist, and also a VPC template to show the necessary NACLs, route tables, and security groups.
[05:33] Omar Khalid: About PrivateLink — does it require a public NLB on your side? How does that impact security posture?
[05:39] Rafael Ortega: Technically PrivateLink uses an NLB in the service provider account to front the service. But the NLB can be internal-only (not internet-facing) and traffic flows over AWS's private network. You must accept endpoint connections in your account. The main operational impact is you need to manage endpoint permissions and the NLB's security group rules on our side.
[05:59] Priya Singh: If we use peering, do you support transitive routing? We avoid transitive peering usually.
[06:05] Rafael Ortega: VPC peering is not transitive; that's why transit gateway or PrivateLink is recommended for complex topologies. If you're using TGW, you can centralize attachments and avoid many peerings. We'll provide TGW patterns we've used.
[06:19] Ben Carter: Any special requirements for IPv6? We're starting to enable IPv6 in some VPCs.
[06:25] Rafael Ortega: We have IPv6 support in preview in certain regions. We'll flag that in the follow-up — depends on model image registries and our NLB support for IPv6.
[06:36] Speaker 6: (quiet) ok
[06:40] Lena Park: Could you walk through an example architecture at a high level for us? Assume we use Transit Gateway and want EU-only traffic.
[06:47] Rafael Ortega: Sure. Example pattern: Redwood service VPC in eu-west-1 hosts the model-serving cluster behind internal NLBs. Your accounts attach to a Transit Gateway which peers to the Redwood TGW attachment (or you peer VPCs directly if small). For PrivateLink, we create an endpoint service in our account; you create an interface endpoint in your consumer VPCs. DNS can be private hosted zones pointing to the interface ENIs. Control plane endpoints (if separate) can be placed in a management VPC with restrictive security groups and only allowed from your admin bastion.
[07:20] Maya Chen: We'll send an architecture diagram — link in notes: https://drive.redwood/arch/aurora-vpc-design.pdf
[07:27] Omar Khalid: For peering versus PrivateLink cost — PrivateLink costs per-hour for ENIs and data processing charges. How do you usually advise customers who are cost-sensitive?
[07:36] Rafael Ortega: If you have only a few VPCs, peering is cheaper; for many accounts at scale, PrivateLink or TGW centralization reduces operational overhead even if it costs a bit more per GB. We'll include a cost comparison spreadsheet.
[07:51] Priya Singh: Any constraints on route table sizes or number of routes added by your endpoints? Some of our VPCs are already close to limits.
[07:58] Rafael Ortega: PrivateLink minimizes route table changes because it's interface-based; peering requires routes to the peer CIDRs. TGW route limits apply — we'll review your route counts during the deep-dive.
[08:12] Lena Park: The pilot — what's the minimum footprint? We want to test with 2 small models and 1 medium model, about 50 concurrent connections for burst.
[08:20] Rafael Ortega: For a pilot we usually provision a small dedicated pool in eu-west-1, reserve a couple of GPUs for the initial test and configure model pinning. We'll provide an acceptance criteria doc: p99 latency under X ms and throughput targets.
[08:36] Ben Carter: Do you need IAM cross-account roles for metrics forwarding or will logs be pushed to our S3?
[08:43] Rafael Ortega: We support both — metrics can be pushed out or you can pull via an assumed role. For security conscious setups, we push logs to an S3 bucket you own.
[08:52] Priya Singh: About endpoint authorization — can we restrict which subnets/endpoints can talk to specific models? We use per-team VPC segmentation.
[08:59] Rafael Ortega: Yes, security groups and internal routing will enforce subnet-level access. We also have per-route/method RBAC at the control plane for API keys and service accounts.
[09:12] Speaker 6: Okay this is helpful
[09:16] Maya Chen: Quick recap and next steps — we'll send VPC Terraform templates, security pack with SOC2, the architecture diagram, and a proposed pilot runbook including benchmark scripts. Rafael will run the network deep-dive next week.
[09:30] Lena Park: Great, please include specific IPs to whitelist and the exact DNS records we should expect. Also include a timeline for a pilot.
[09:38] Maya Chen: Will do. Any final questions?
[09:42] Priya Singh: One more— how do you handle audit logging retention? We need 1 year by default and archival for 7 years.
[09:49] Rafael Ortega: We can forward logs to your S3 with lifecycle rules for your retention; the control plane also keeps short-term logs — we'll document retention options.
[09:58] Omar Khalid: And who at Redwood will be the hands-on contact during pilot?
[10:02] Maya Chen: Rafael will be lead SE and I'll be AE owner. I'll put names in the next steps.
[10:08] Ben Carter: Thanks all
[10:10] Lena Park: Thanks, talk soon.

[10:20] End of transcript (approx 52 min)

Notes and links: architecture diagram: https://drive.redwood/arch/aurora-vpc-design.pdf; security pack (SOC2 + KMS guide): https://drive.redwood/security/aurora-security-pack.zip; cost comparison spreadsheet placeholder: https://docs.redwood/costs/aurora-comparison.xlsx
